title: Cells of the walking adjunction relative to one triangle
statement:
Use simplicial sets, nerves, standard simplices and horns of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. A simplicial category has simplicial hom-sets, identity vertices and strictly associative unital simplicial composition; a simplicial functor preserves this structure. For a simplicial set $X$, define its right cone $X^{\triangleright}$ by adjoining a last vertex $*$: its $r$-simplices are the constant simplex at $*$ and the disjoint union of $X_j$ for $0\leq j\leq r$, with the copy of $X_j$ occupying the initial $j+1$ vertices and all remaining vertices equal to $*$. Operators restrict or repeat the initial block, giving the constant apex when that block becomes empty. Define $2[X]$ to have objects $0,1$, hom $2[X](0,1)=X$, identity homs $\Delta^0$ and reverse hom empty. Define $3[X]$ to have objects $0,1,2$, homs $3[X](0,1)=X$, $3[X](1,2)=\Delta^0$, $3[X](0,2)=X^{\triangleright}$, identity homs $\Delta^0$ and all other homs empty, with composition $X\to X^{\triangleright}$ the initial inclusion.

Let $\mathsf{Adj}$ be the simplicial category obtained by applying the nerve to each hom-category of the free strict $2$-category generated by objects $+,-$, arrows $\ell:+\to-$, $u:-\to+$, unit $\eta:1_+\to u\ell$ and counit $\epsilon:\ell u\to1_-$, with the two triangle identities. Let $\beta$ denote its $2$-simplex with successive edges $\ell\eta,\epsilon\ell$ and long edge the identity at $\ell$. The simplicial subcategory $A_0\subseteq\mathsf{Adj}$ generated under composition, faces and degeneracies by $\ell,u,\eta,\epsilon,\beta$ has the following freeness property: a simplicial functor from $A_0$ into any simplicial category is determined by arbitrary images of those generators having the indicated boundaries, with no additional relations beyond those boundaries and the simplicial-category axioms.

There is an increasing sequence $A_0\subseteq A_1\subseteq\cdots$ of simplicial subcategories with union $\mathsf{Adj}$. Each inclusion $A_i\to A_{i+1}$ is a pushout of a finite coproduct of maps of the following two types: (i) $2[\Lambda_k^n]\to2[\Delta^n]$ with $n\geq2$ and $0<k<n$; (ii) $3[\partial\Delta^m]\to3[\Delta^m]$ with $m\geq1$. Here $\partial\Delta^m$ is the union of all proper faces. For every attachment of type (ii), the attaching map into $A_i$ sends the objects $0,1,2$ to $b,+,-$ for $b\in\{+,-\}$, sends $1\to2$ to $\ell$, sends the last vertex $m$ in the $0\to1$ hom to $ua$, sends the cone apex in the $0\to2$ hom to $a$, and sends the cone edge from $m$ to that apex to $\epsilon a$, where $a=1_-$ if $b=-$ and $a=\ell$ if $b=+$.

source.place: Riehl--Verity, Homotopy coherent adjunctions and the formal theory of monads: Example 4.2.3; Lemma 4.2.10, Corollary 4.2.13, Proposition 4.2.15; the final-edge calculation in the proof of Theorem 4.3.8, pp. 834--845. Online source read; archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag supplies this simplicial-computad calculation.

proof.text: Work in the string model of [lem-coef-adjunction-squiggle-normal-form]. The faces of $\beta=(-,2,1,+)$ are $\ell\eta,s_0\ell,\epsilon\ell$. The faces of $\eta$ and $\epsilon$ are words in $\ell,u$ and identities. Thus the words of degeneracies of the five atoms $\ell,u,\eta,\epsilon,\beta$ form a simplicial subcategory closed under taking atomic factors. It is precisely the stated $A_0$: it contains the generators, and closure of this set of words proves the reverse inclusion. Given their arbitrary images with these boundaries, define the image of a general arrow by its unique word of degeneracies. Uniqueness of the normal form makes this well-defined and forces preservation of composition and degeneracies. For faces, expand the face of each atomic generator using the listed boundaries; simplicial identities give the same expansion on its degeneracies, and faces preserve the word composition. Hence this defines a simplicial functor with no further relations. This proves the freeness assertion, including existence.

source.place: Example 4.2.3 and Proposition 2.2.6, derived here from the string normal form

proof.text: Call a factor-closed simplicial subcategory parental when it contains $\ell$ and, for every nonfillable nondegenerate atom it contains, it also contains that atom's fillable parent. By [lem-coef-adjunction-fillable-parent-bijection], the parents of $u$ and $\eta$ are respectively $\epsilon$ and $\beta$ (substitute their strings from [lem-coef-adjunction-squiggle-normal-form]). The other three initial atoms are fillable, so $A_0$ is parental. Every missing nonfillable atom has a unique fillable parent; thus it suffices to exhaust the fillable atoms. Put $\rho(a)=(w(a),k(a),\dim a)$, with $k(\ell)=0$. Enumerate in increasing lexicographic order the nonempty sets $X_i$ of fillable atoms outside $A_0$ having the same rank. These sets are finite: for fixed width the normal-form lemma bounds the dimension by $w-1$ and gives finitely many strings. Each rank has only finitely many preceding possible ranks, since $1\leq k\leq n<w$ away from $\ell$. This gives a sequence indexed by natural numbers, rather than a longer ordinal; if it terminates, repeat the last stage using empty coproducts.

source.place: Definitions 4.2.1--4.2.2, Example 4.2.3, and finite lexicographic indexing in Proposition 4.2.15

proof.text: Inductively maintain that $A_i$ is parental and contains $A_0$ and all fillable atoms at ranks before $X_i$, together with their children. The base case was just checked. For $a\in X_i$, every face except $d_{k(a)}a$ is already in $A_i$: [lem-coef-adjunction-nondistinguished-face-rank] expresses each of its nondegenerate atomic factors either as an earlier fillable atom or as an earlier fillable atom's child; take its degeneracies and then their word. If such an earlier parent is in $A_0$, its child is in $A_0$ as a face, or as an atomic factor of $d_n a=\ell a^-$; factor closure handles the latter. The child $a^-$ itself is absent from $A_i$, because parentality would otherwise put its unique parent $a$ in $A_i$. Distinct $a\in X_i$ have distinct children by the parent bijection. The children are nonfillable, so none is another member of $X_i$.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.15: induction and nondistinguished-face membership; Lemma 4.2.10: absence of the child

proof.text: Let $B$ consist of words of degeneracies of the old nondegenerate atoms and the new pairs $a,a^-$ for $a\in X_i$. Faces of each new parent other than the distinguished one are old by step 3; the distinguished face is $a^-$ or $\ell a^-$. Faces of each child are old: if $k<n$, apply the simplicial face identities to $a^-=d_k a$; each double face can be written using a face of $a$ other than $d_k a$. If $k=n$, the same identities show that $\ell d_j a^-$ is old for every $j$; factor closure then gives $d_j a^-$ old. The normal form now shows that $B$ is closed under faces, degeneracies, composition and atomic factors. Its nondegenerate atoms are exactly the old atoms and those pairs. It is parental, since each new nonfillable atom is paired with its new fillable parent. Set $A_{i+1}=B$. This proves the induction hypothesis at the successor; it also proves there are no unlisted new generators or relations at this stage.

source.place: Lemma 4.2.10 and Corollary 4.2.13: the two new atomic arrows and parental closure

proof.text: For a new $n$-arrow $a$ with depth $0<k<n$, the hom simplex $a$ induces $2[\Delta^n]\to A_{i+1}$. All faces other than $k$ land in $A_i$, so this restricts to an attaching map $2[\Lambda_k^n]\to A_i$. For any target simplicial category $K$ and functor $F:A_i\to K$, an extension across this pair is exactly the choice of an $n$-simplex $x$ in the appropriate hom of $K$ with $d_jx=F(d_ja)$ for $j\ne k$; the image of the child is forced to be $d_kx$. The unique-word normal form makes these choices both sufficient and unique for extending the functor, by the same face check as step 1. This is exactly the universal property of attaching $2[\Delta^n]$ along its inner horn. The depth inequalities force $n\geq2$.

source.place: Definition 4.2.9 and Lemma 4.2.10, pushout (4.2.11), including its universal-property proof

proof.text: For a new $n$-arrow $a$ with depth $n$, let $b$ be its source. Map $3[\Delta^{n-1}]$ to $A_{i+1}$ by sending objects to $b,+,-$, its $1\to2$ hom to $\ell$, the top $(n-1)$-simplex of its $0\to1$ hom to $a^-$, and the top $n$-simplex of its cone hom to $a$. The equality $d_na=\ell a^-$ is exactly compatibility with composition. Step 3 and the child-face check in step 4 show that $3[\partial\Delta^{n-1}]$ lands in $A_i$. For a target $K$ and $F:A_i\to K$, an extension is exactly a pair of simplices $y$ of dimension $n-1$ and $x$ of dimension $n$, with the prescribed old faces and $d_nx=F(\ell)y$. This is exactly a functor from $3[\Delta^{n-1}]$ agreeing on its boundary; normal form extends it uniquely on words. Hence this is the type (ii) pushout. The only fillable $1$-arrow is $\epsilon=(-,1,-)$, already in $A_0$; $\ell$ is also old. Consequently all these attachments have $n\geq2$, so $m=n-1\geq1$.

source.place: Definition 4.2.9 and Lemma 4.2.10, pushout (4.2.12), including its universal-property proof

proof.text: For a fixed finite $X_i$, combine the choices in steps 5 and 6. Distinct pairs have no common new atom, and every boundary condition other than the stated relation $d_na=\ell a^-$ is old. Thus a functor from $A_{i+1}$ is equivalent to a functor from $A_i$ together with one compatible functor from each cell codomain, agreeing on each cell domain. This is the pushout universal property for their finite coproduct, with the attaching object maps allowed to identify objects. Finally every fillable atom is in $A_0$ or some $X_i$, and every nonfillable atom is the child of one by [lem-coef-adjunction-fillable-parent-bijection]. Every arrow is a finite word of degeneracies of atoms by the normal-form lemma, so it lies in a common finite stage. The increasing union is therefore the whole $\mathsf{Adj}$.

source.place: Corollary 4.2.13 and Proposition 4.2.15: finite simultaneous cells and exhaustion

proof.text: It remains to identify the boundary data for a type (ii) cell. Its fillable parent has string $a=(-,n,a_2,\ldots,a_w)$, with every other internal letter strictly less than $n$. Restriction to its last edge $\{n-1,n\}$ sends each letter below $n$ to $-$, the letter $n$ to $1$, and $+$ to $+$. Thus the resulting string is $(-,1,-,\ldots,-)$ for source $-$ and $(-,1,-,\ldots,-,+)$ for source $+$. Alternation fixes the endpoint parity, so cancellation of adjacent equal pairs gives respectively $(-,1,-)=\epsilon$ and $(-,1,-,+)=\epsilon\ell$. The last vertex (the cone apex) is therefore $1_-$ or $\ell$; call it $v$. Before the cone, the last vertex of $a^-$ is $u$ or $u\ell$: delete the leading $\ell$ from $d_na$, or apply the same letter restriction to its string. Hence it is $uv$, and the final cone edge is $\epsilon v$. Renaming $v$ as the $a$ in the statement gives exactly its last-vertex, apex and counit formulas. Since $m\geq1$, all these vertices and the last cone edge already belong to the attaching boundary. The object and $\ell$ assignments were fixed explicitly in step 6.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 4.3.8, p. 845: explicit restriction to the last edge and its two source cases

Instead I checked every claim against my own implementation of the string model. The model is right: the simplicial identities hold, every hom is a nerve (an n-simplex is determined by its spine), and the hom-category counts give N(Δ+), N(Δ+)^op and C(m+p,m) for the two mixed homs, matching W=N(Δ_∞). β=(-,2,1,+) has faces ℓη, s0ℓ and εℓ. Parent bijection, over all atoms of dimension ≤4 and width ≤9: the only fillable atoms of dimension ≤1 are ℓ and ε; the d_k child for k<n and the ℓa^- child for k=n have the stated widths; the inverse formula returns each of 186 fillables exactly and works for all 239 nonfillables of dimension ≤3; u†=ε and η†=β. The factorwise rank inequality holds in all 1379 factor checks, including identity faces. The last-edge calculation holds in all 74 cases: εv with v=1_- or ℓ, and the last vertex of the child is uv. Item steps 1–8: A_0 is closed under faces, degeneracies and factors and its words define functors uniquely. Rank classes are finite with finitely many predecessors, so the sequence is ω-indexed. Nondistinguished faces are old because the rank inequality is strict. Faces of the child are old by d_j d_k = d_{k-1} d_j (j<k), d_j d_k = d_k d_{j+1} (j≥k), and factor closure when k=n. The functor-extension arguments for 2[Λ^n_k] and 3[∂Δ^m] are correct, with n≥2 and m≥1 because ε and ℓ are already in A_0. The steps marked elementary (2, 7, 8) are elementary. The parent uses exactly the clauses provided. No duplicates in the DAG (bead normal form and relative cells concern C[K]; weight cells concern a D-module) or in the blueprint.
